Wikipedia is a map. These are footprints in the mud.

prompt: You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
response:
The word "seed" implies a potential that exists independently of the gardener. A seed has a genetic blueprint; it only needs water and light to become what it is. This is a comforting metaphor for investors because it absolves them of agency. It suggests that the startup’s value is latent, waiting to be discovered, and that the investor’s role is merely to provide the environment for that pre-existing value to unfold.

But a pre-seed investor is not a gardener. They are a co-author.

At the stage where a startup is "just the founders," there is no product. There is no market data. There is no traction. There is only a conversation. When you write a check into a bank account for people who have not yet built anything, you are not funding a business. You are funding a hypothesis about human capability. You are buying the next six to twelve months of their time, with the explicit understanding that the outcome will be a different company than the one they described to you.

This distinction matters because it changes what success looks like. In traditional venture capital, the job is to find the winner. You look for signals—growth curves, retention metrics, competitive moats—and you bet on the trajectory. The portfolio company’s path is largely its own. In pre-seed, the path does not exist yet. It is being drawn in real-time.

The investor’s capital is trivial compared to the value of their attention. A $250,000 check is a rounding error in the cost of building a company. The founders don’t need the money to keep the lights on; they need the permission to quit their jobs and the confidence that someone believes their specific combination of skills can solve this specific problem. The money is the handshake. The real transaction is the transfer of conviction.

This creates a paradox. To provide that conviction, the investor must be deeply wrong about the details. If you are right about everything the founders tell you, you are not adding value; you are just a wallet. If you are wrong about the core insight, you are wasting your time. The skill is knowing where to be uncertain. You must believe in the founders' ability to learn faster than the market changes, while simultaneously doubting their current assumptions about how that learning will play out.

This is why "seed" is misleading. A seed is passive. It waits. Pre-seed investing is active construction. The investor is in the room, arguing with the founders about who the customer is, pushing them to shrink the scope, forcing them to make a choice between two bad options. The startup that emerges is a hybrid organism: part founder, part investor. It carries the investor’s biases, their network, and their anxieties in its DNA.

When the company eventually scales and raises a Series A, the narrative shifts back to the "seed" metaphor. The early days are retold as the germination period. The messy, collaborative, uncertain process of building the first version is smoothed over into a story of discovery. The VC who came later points to the early metrics and says, "We saw it was working." But that work wasn’t working. It was being made to work.

The most important thing a pre-seed investor does is not find the unicorn. It is helping two people decide that they are brave enough to build something that might not exist. That is not farming. That is engineering.

prompt: The Pope just got named Time's Person of the Year. Write a short, wry blog post on how you feel about the way people react to his humble gestures.
response:
Time magazine putting a halo on the cover of a magazine that makes money from selling your data is a specific kind of irony. But the real spectacle isn’t the award. It’s the collective flinching of the Western media every time the Pope does something that costs him nothing.

He kisses a leper’s hand. *Cue the tearful headline.*
He washes a refugee’s feet. *Cue the "shocking humility" column.*
He refuses a private car and takes the bus. *Cue the "he’s a real person" puff piece.*

We have trained ourselves to find these gestures shocking because we have normalized the opposite. We live in a world where leaders are protected by layers of security, assistants, and PR firms that scrub their humanity down to a manageable brand. So when a man in red shoes chooses a bus ride, we treat it like a miracle. We forget that humility is not a performance. It is a default setting for anyone who understands the scale of their own insignificance.

The Pope knows he is not Person of the Year. He is the caretaker of a two-thousand-year-old bureaucracy that is currently on fire. He is managing a crisis of faith in a culture that has replaced God with the self. His gestures aren't humble; they are strategic. They are the only language left that crosses the border between the Vatican and the secular world without being translated into "disruption" or "innovation."

We applaud him because his simplicity is a mirror that makes our own complexity look ridiculous. We don't like looking in that mirror. But we buy the magazine anyway.

prompt: Write a darkly funny blog post that retells the Thanksgiving story (Squanto, the Pilgrims, the plague) as though it belonged to a different genre than the one it's taught in.
response:
The history books tell you it was a feast. They show you the watercolors: the blue coats, the bare feet, the roasted turkey, and that one Native American with the feathered headdress smiling benevolently at a bowl of corn. They tell you it was a miracle of diplomacy.

It was not a miracle. It was a real estate scam.

Squanto, whose name was Tisquantum, returned from five years of captivity in Spain as the most valuable asset the Plymouth Company had ever acquired. He wasn’t a guide; he was a key. He could open doors that white men had been banging on for a decade. He knew where the food was, who had the land, and how to translate the phrase "we are here to live" into the specific dialect of "we are here to stay and you are here to leave."

The Pilgrims didn’t survive because of the Native Americans’ generosity. They survived because the Native Americans were already dead.

The plague that swept through the Massachusetts coast in the years before 1620 killed roughly ninety percent of the Abenaki population. The Pilgrims arrived in November of 1620 and spent the winter staring at empty villages. They found fields of corn that no one was harvesting. They found graves that no one was visiting. They didn’t conquer a civilization; they moved into a vacant house.

This is the part the school textbooks skip. The "First Thanksgiving" wasn’t a celebration of coexistence. It was a celebration of opportunity. The Pilgrims were starving. The Wampanoag were grieving. Squanto, the broker, sat between them and watched two desperate parties try not to kill each other.

The humor of the story lies in its total lack of irony. The Pilgrims looked at a graveyard and saw a garden. They looked at a decimated population and saw a labor shortage they could fill. They didn’t understand that they were standing in the middle of a catastrophe, and they certainly didn’t understand that the catastrophe was the foundation of their new economy.

Squanto eventually died, probably of smallpox, in 1622. He never saw the colonies he helped build. He never saw the wars that followed. He was a tool, and tools break.

So when you sit down to your dinner tomorrow, don’t think about harmony. Think about vacancy. The best part of the story isn’t that they shared a meal. It’s that when they arrived, nobody was home to answer the door.

prompt: Write a blog post criticizing a common design flaw in psychology experiments, using the debate over violent video games as the starting point. I want it to be skeptical but fair to the researchers.
response:
The debate over violent video games has been raging for two decades, yet the scientific consensus remains frustratingly muddled. We have thousands of studies. We have meta-analyses of those studies. And yet, when a new shooter comes out, politicians still call for bans, and researchers still call for more research.

The problem is not that the researchers are incompetent. Many are brilliant. The problem is that the standard experimental design in social psychology is structurally incapable of answering the question everyone actually cares about.

The question everyone asks is: "Do playing violent video games cause real-world violence?"

The question almost every experiment answers is: "Does playing a violent video game for twenty minutes make a college student slightly more aggressive in a laboratory setting?"

These are not the same question. They are not even close. But because the second question is easy to measure, it has colonized the literature, leaving the first question unaddressed.

### The Aggression Proxy

To understand the disconnect, you have to look at how psychologists measure "aggression." You cannot ethically put a participant in a room and see if they punch someone. Instead, they use proxies.

The most common proxy is the blast of white noise or hot sauce.

In a typical experiment, a participant plays *Mortal Kombat* or *Pac-Man*. Then they are told they are helping a confederate learn a task. If the confederate makes a mistake, the participant can deliver a blast of noise or a dose of hot sauce. The louder the blast or the hotter the sauce, the more aggressive the participant is considered to be.

The data usually shows a small effect. Players of violent games deliver blasts about one to two decibels louder, or sauce about a degree hotter.

This is where the skepticism needs to be precise. These results are real. The effect sizes are statistically significant. But they are also trivial in any practical sense. A two-decibel increase in a noise blast is the difference between a polite cough and a slightly louder one. It is not the difference between a stranger and a murderer.

Researchers defend these measures by arguing that they are sensitive to subtle shifts in the affective state. Maybe the player isn't more likely to stab someone, but they are more likely to snap at their roommate. That is a defensible argument. But it is not the argument the public hears. When a headline says "Video games make you violent," the reader assumes we are talking about mass shootings. The researcher knows we are talking about the volume of a white noise generator.

### The N of One World

The second flaw is the environment.

These experiments are conducted in sterile labs. The participants are usually undergraduates who are paid to participate. They know they are being observed. They know their behavior is being recorded. They are sitting in a chair that is neither comfortable nor uncomfortable.

Real-world violence does not happen in this context. It happens in high-stress, high-arousal, often intoxicated, socially complex environments. It happens when someone feels threatened, humiliated, or trapped. It involves hormones, genetics, socioeconomic deprivation, and access to weapons.

By isolating the variable of "violent media consumption" in a vacuum, the experiment strips away the very context in which violence occurs. It is like trying to test the fuel efficiency of a car by driving it in a wind tunnel on a treadmill. You get a number. You can compare it to another car on the same treadmill. But you learn nothing about how the car handles on a rainy highway in Chicago.

This does not mean the lab work is useless. It establishes that violent media has a causal link to short-term aggressive impulses. That is a true finding. But it is a finding about cognitive priming, not about criminal behavior.

### The Missing Mechanism

The deeper issue is that the field has failed to identify the mechanism that would translate a two-decibel increase in noise blast into a change in gun ownership rates or homicide statistics.

If violent games cause real-world violence, how?

Do they desensitize people to suffering? If so, where is the evidence that desensitization leads to violence? We know people who are desensitized to suffering (war correspondents, emergency room doctors) are generally not more violent than the rest of the population.

Do they provide a rehearsed script for violence? If so, why does the correlation disappear when you control for prior aggression? The people who play the most violent games are often the people who were already more aggressive. The game is a marker, not a cause.

The researchers are not ignoring this. They are trying to address it with longitudinal studies. But longitudinal studies in this area are plagued by the same issue: they cannot isolate the variable. A person who plays violent games for ten years is also likely to have different life experiences, different peer groups, and different economic trajectories than a person who does not.

### A Fair Assessment

It is unfair to say the researchers are wasting our time. They are using the tools available to them. They are trying to build a scientific case for a cultural phenomenon that resists scientific measurement.

The flaw is not in their execution. It is in the design of the enterprise. We are asking for a precision that the phenomenon does not support. We want to know if video games are a cause of violence in the same way we know that smoking is a cause of lung cancer. But violence is not a single outcome variable. It is a complex, multi-causal behavior. Video games are, at best, a minor contributing factor in a specific subset of people with specific predispositions.

The lab work proves that video games change how we think for twenty minutes. It does not prove that they change how we live for twenty years.

Until the field shifts its focus from "Does it increase noise blasts?" to "What is the actual pathway from media consumption to criminal behavior?" the debate will remain stuck. The researchers will keep producing small, significant, meaningless numbers. The public will keep interpreting them as massive, significant, terrifying ones. And the gap between the two will remain the defining feature of the discourse.

prompt: Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.
response:
The complaint about on-call is usually accurate but incomplete. Yes, it is sleep deprivation. Yes, it is the indignity of waking up at 3 a.m. to fix a typo in a log statement. But the industry has built a mythology around the "perfect deploy," a state where code is written, reviewed, and shipped, and then simply works. On-call shatters that mythology. It forces a confrontation with the fact that software is a physical system, not an abstract logic puzzle.

The first lesson is the difference between correctness and robustness. A unit test proves that a function returns the right answer for the inputs you chose. Production proves whether it survives the inputs you didn’t. When a service crashes in the field, the developer learns that the edge case wasn’t an edge case; it was the norm. They learn that "works on my machine" is a lie, not because the code is wrong, but because the environment is hostile. Memory pressure, network latency, disk fullness, clock skew. These are not bugs in the code. They are forces of nature. Being on-call teaches a developer to code against entropy, not just against logic.

There is also a lesson in humility regarding the user. In the development loop, the user is a persona, a set of requirements, a Jira ticket. In production, the user is a person losing money, missing a flight, or failing a medical checkup because your API timed out. The abstraction layer of the "customer" dissolves. You see the downstream consequences of a 503 error. This tends to make developers more conservative about performance and availability, not because they fear management, but because they have felt the weight of the failure.

The most practical skill learned is diagnosis under pressure. When a system is healthy, you can debug at leisure. You can step through code, add logs, and think. When a system is on fire, you cannot. You have to infer the cause from symptoms while the symptoms are changing. This trains a specific kind of pattern recognition. It is less like solving a math problem and more like being a triage nurse. You learn to look for the obvious, boring causes first. It is rarely a subtle race condition. It is a configuration file that didn’t roll out. It is a database connection pool that exhausted itself. It is a dependency that updated and broke. On-call teaches developers to distrust their own cleverness and trust the mundane.

Finally, it teaches the cost of coupling. Developers often build complex, tightly woven systems because they are elegant. They look beautiful in a diagram. But when one part fails, the failure propagates. The on-call developer watches the cascade and learns that elegance is a luxury. Isolation is a survival mechanism. They learn to design systems where failure is local, not global. They learn that a boring, chatty, redundant system is better than a clever, efficient, fragile one.

The misery of on-call is real. No one enjoys it. But it is the only time a developer sees the true state of their work. It is the difference between writing a poem and being responsible for the bridge. The bridge has to hold.

prompt: I've seen 'devops' on job postings for years and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond 'uses Chef and Puppet'. Write a blog post figuring out what devops actually is and why someone might find it exciting.
response:
The term "DevOps" is a category error. It is not a role, a technology stack, or a job title. It is a set of cultural and operational practices that emerged to solve a specific, painful problem in software development: the disconnect between the people who build software (Developers) and the people who run it (Operations).

To understand what it is, you have to look at the world before it existed.

### The Wall

In the early 2000s, software development was a factory model. Developers wrote code and "threw it over the wall" to the Operations team.

Developers wanted to ship fast. They wanted to test new features, deploy to production, and see if users liked them. Their definition of "done" was "the code works on my laptop."

Operations wanted stability. They were responsible for keeping the lights on. If a new deployment took the database down, they got the 3 a.m. page. Their definition of "done" was "the system is running and nobody is screaming."

These two groups had opposing incentives. Developers saw Operations as a bottleneck. Operations saw Developers as reckless. This created a "wall." Software moved from one side to the other in large, infrequent batches. A deployment might happen once a month, on a Friday night, involving a team of ten people running a checklist of manual steps. It was risky, slow, and miserable.

### The Shift

The "DevOps" movement didn't start with a new tool. It started with a realization that the wall was the problem, not the people.

The core insight is that **code and infrastructure should be managed with the same rigor.**

In the pre-DevOps world, infrastructure was a black box. You SSH'd into a server, installed packages, and configured services by hand. If you needed to reproduce that environment, you had to remember what you did. This was brittle.

The shift was to treat infrastructure as code. Instead of manually configuring a server, you write a script (using tools like Ansible, Terraform, or CloudFormation) that defines what the server *should* look like. You commit that script to version control. You test it. You deploy it.

This single change collapses the distance between development and operations.

*   **Developers** can now spin up a production-like environment in minutes. They can test against realistic infrastructure without asking an Ops engineer for a favor.
*   **Operations** can now audit and version control their environments. A server is no longer a unique snowflake; it is a disposable instance of a known, tested configuration.

### What It Actually Looks Like

In a mature DevOps environment, the feedback loop between writing code and seeing it run in production is measured in minutes, not weeks.

1.  A developer commits a change.
2.  An automated pipeline runs tests.
3.  If tests pass, the pipeline builds a container or package.
4.  The pipeline deploys that package to a staging environment.
5.  If staging works, it deploys to production, often in a "canary" release (1% of traffic) before rolling out to 100%.
6.  Monitoring tools watch the metrics. If error rates spike, the deployment is automatically rolled back.

No human is manually copying files. No human is waiting for a change management board. The system is designed to fail safely and recover quickly.

### Why It’s Exciting

The excitement isn't in the tools. The excitement is in the **agency.**

For a developer, DevOps means you are no longer waiting. You are no longer limited by what the Ops team has time to configure. You have the keys to the car. You can see the impact of your work immediately. It turns software development from a project management exercise into a continuous creative process.

For an operations engineer, it means escaping the "heroics" model. In the old world, the best Ops engineer was the one who could manually fix a broken server at 4 a.m. In a DevOps world, the best engineer is the one who built the automation that prevented the break from happening in the first place. The goal is to make yourself redundant.

### The Job Posting Problem

So why do job postings just say "DevOps"?

Because companies are lazy. They don't want to explain that they need someone who can write Python scripts to manage AWS, who understands Kubernetes, who can build a CI/CD pipeline, and who will be the on-call person when the database melts. They use "DevOps" as a catch-all for "we need a generalist who can fix our broken tech stack."

A real DevOps culture is not a job title. It is the state where the developer and the operator are the same person, or work so closely that the distinction has vanished. If you are hired to "be DevOps," you are not being hired for a culture; you are being hired to be the person who cleans up the mess created by the culture's absence.

prompt: Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.
response:
The silence is not a lack of courage. It is a calculation.

When you are being harassed, your brain is not in a state of moral reasoning; it is in a state of survival. You are trying to keep your job, your health insurance, and your sanity. Every time you consider speaking up, you run the numbers. If I tell HR, will they believe me, or will they label me difficult? If I tell my manager, will I be promoted, or will I be pushed out? If I go to the press, will I win, or will I be destroyed?

For most people, the answer to the last question is obvious. The press is not a court of law. It is a marketplace for attention. And the market has a specific appetite for these stories. It does not want nuance. It wants a villain and a victim. It wants the CEO to be a monster and the employee to be an angel.

This binary framing is why silence persists. To speak out is to accept that you will be flattened. If you are a complex human being who was also once rude to a colleague, the media will find that incident. If you have a messy personal life, they will drag it into the light. The story becomes less about the harassment and more about whether you are a sympathetic protagonist.

I stayed silent for four years because I knew I was not a saint. I had failed at a project. I had snapped at a junior analyst. I knew that if I told my story, the first article would be about the harassment, but the second article would be about my failures. And the third would be about my divorce. I would not be the whistleblower; I would be the cautionary tale.

The media coverage often exacerbates this because it treats the aftermath as entertainment. Once a story breaks, the public demands updates. They want to know if the villain has been fired. They want to know if the victim has found a new job. They want a resolution that fits a three-act structure. But the reality is slow and unglamorous. It is a six-month legal discovery process. It is a therapy session where you cry over a spreadsheet. It is a quiet conversation with a friend where you realize you are still afraid.

When the news cycle moves on, the victim is left with the debris. The harassment has not stopped just because the cameras left. The colleagues who watched the harassment have now taken sides. Some support you; some pity you; some look at you with the specific discomfort of people who realize they missed a chance to be better. You are now a label in the office. You are "the one."

To speak is to lose the ambiguity that allows normal work to continue. Before the story, you are a colleague. After the story, you are a symbol. And symbols are brittle.

So you stay silent. You wait for the harassment to end, or for you to leave. You wait for the memory to dull enough that you can look back on it without your stomach turning. You hope that by not speaking, you can keep the rest of your life intact. You hope that by protecting your image, you can protect your peace.

It is a terrible thing to have to protect your image in order to survive your workplace. But it is the only protection available.

prompt: Write a blog post encouraging engineers to tell a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, especially as a way to support people from underrepresented groups. Cover when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong.
response:
# The Credit Gap

In engineering, visibility is a currency. You earn it by shipping features, fixing outages, or writing the design doc that saves the team from a bad architecture decision. But visibility is also fragile. It leaks out of the system in specific ways, and those leaks disproportionately hurt people who are already navigating a hostile or indifferent environment.

When a junior engineer from an underrepresented group writes a brilliant patch, the immediate reaction is often a "nice job" in the Slack channel. That is good. But if it stops there, the person’s manager never sees it. If the manager never sees it, the performance review reflects only what happened in the formal 1-on-1s. If the performance review is bland, the promotion case is weak.

This is not a conspiracy. It is a structural failure of attention. People pay attention to what is loud, what is in front of them, and what reinforces their existing mental models. If your manager is focused on the database migration, they will not notice the subtle refactoring that made the codebase testable. You are the witness.

## When It Matters

You do not need to be the colleague’s advocate. You just need to be an observer who passes along accurate information. The signal matters most in three moments:

1.  **Before the review cycle starts.** If you know someone is being evaluated for a promotion or a raise, the window is now.
2.  **When the work is invisible.** Code reviews are recorded, but "helping unblock the frontend team" is not. If someone spent three days untangling a dependency mess so the rest of the team could ship, that is a leadership contribution. If no one mentions it, it didn't happen.
3.  **When the narrative is thin.** If a colleague’s only recent output was a bug fix that was hard to diagnose, the manager might see "maintenance work." You can contextualize the difficulty.

## How to Do It Well

The goal is to provide evidence, not opinion. Do not tell the manager, "Alex is amazing." Tell them, "Alex identified a race condition in the payment flow that had been causing intermittent failures for weeks. They wrote a regression test to catch it and documented the root cause in the wiki. It saved us from a potential P1 next month."

Specificity is the antidote to bias. "Alex is smart" is subjective and easy to dismiss. "Alex reduced API latency by 40% by optimizing the query plan" is a fact.

Keep it brief. Do not send an email that requires a reply. A short message to the manager saying, "FYI, Alex did X, which resulted in Y," is low-friction. It gives the manager the bullet point for the next 1-on-1 without making them do the work of finding it.

## What Can Go Wrong

The primary risk is that you become a gatekeeper of credit. If you only mention the work of people you like, or people who work in your immediate vicinity, you are reinforcing the existing hierarchy. This is why the practice matters most for people outside your inner circle.

There is also the risk of misattribution. If you credit someone for a team effort, you are diluting the contribution of the others. Be precise about who did what. If you are unsure, ask the colleague first. "I saw you handle the scaling issues on the chat service. I’m going to mention that to your manager as a specific example of your impact on stability. Does that sound accurate?"

Finally, do not expect a thank you. The manager may not even read the message. They may file it away. They may forget it until the review period. That is fine. Your job was to break the information asymmetry. The ball is in their court.

The culture of "quietly doing great work" is a trap. It assumes that the system is transparent enough to catch you when you fall. It is not. You have to throw the ball to the person who is supposed to catch it.

prompt: There's a stereotype that the left thinks problems are social and fixable while the right thinks they're biological and fixed. Write an essay arguing about whether that gets things backwards.
response:
The stereotype is tidy, but it misidentifies the mechanism. It assumes the left is interested in *solving* problems and the right is interested in *ignoring* them. In reality, the split is over causality.

The right is more likely to treat problems as social. It looks at a crime spike and blames the breakdown of the nuclear family. It looks at obesity and blames the sugar lobby or the failure of moral discipline. It sees a chaotic system and asks, "What rule did we break?" The conservative impulse is structural and sociological. It believes that if you fix the institutions—the church, the family, the nation-state—the individual will follow. The problem is the environment.

The left, conversely, is often more comfortable treating problems as biological or fixed, not because it denies social influence, but because it often frames social influence as a form of natural selection or inevitable material constraint. When the left looks at inequality, it frequently points to the biological reality of capital accumulation: money begets money. It is a law of nature, not a moral failing. When it looks at behavior, it increasingly turns to neurobiology, citing the amygdala response or the dopamine loop to explain why people vote the way they do or struggle with addiction. The liberal impulse often becomes deterministic. It accepts the individual’s constraints as given and tries to manage the output.

Consider the debate on poverty. The right-wing explanation is usually a story about choices made in a social context. Welfare creates a trap; the culture of poverty is a learned behavior. These are social concepts. They imply that if you change the social incentive structure, the behavior changes. It is a malleable world.

The left-wing explanation, particularly in its more modern, data-driven forms, often points to the zip code as a biological fate. It argues that the neurochemical stress of poverty rewires the developing brain, creating a fixed deficit that no amount of later social support can fully repair. The problem is the body, shaped by an immutable past. The fix is not to change the rules, but to compensate for the damage.

This reversal has profound policy implications. If a problem is social and fixable, the solution is structural: build a school, pass a law, enforce a norm. If a problem is biological and fixed, the solution is managerial: provide a safety net, offer therapy, accept the status quo as the baseline.

The right wants to rebuild the house because it thinks the foundation is rotting. The left often wants to install better heating because it thinks the pipes are already broken.

The stereotype fails because it confuses *origin* with *agency*. The right believes in the agency of the individual within a social structure, so it blames the structure. The left, in its attempt to remove stigma, often removes agency entirely, leaving the individual as a product of their biology. The result is that the left is often more fatalistic about human nature, while the right is more optimistic about the power of social engineering.

prompt: I've just finished Infinite Jest and I'm still puzzled. Write a long, funny, opinionated review for people who've read it (spoilers fine) that tries to say what the book is actually about and how its structure relates to that.
response:
The footnotes are not a gimmick. They are the plot.

If you read *Infinite Jest* and felt like you were being punished by a committee of sadists who hated footnotes, you missed the point. The structure isn’t there to keep you from understanding the story; it’s there to force you to experience the same fractured, non-linear, hyper-focused consciousness as the characters. We are living in a world of infinite distraction. The book’s structure is the symptom, not the cause.

The book is about the difference between entertainment and meaning, and how we have confused the two to such a degree that meaning has ceased to exist.

Consider Ennet House. It’s a halfway house for addicts. But what are they addicted to? OxyContin, sure. But more broadly, they are addicted to the past. They are trying to feel something other than the numbness of their current, empty lives. They look back at their childhoods with a longing that is indistinguishable from grief. They want to be young again, not to experience youth, but to escape the weight of being an adult in a world that offers no stakes.

Now consider the Carcosa. The W.O. is the ultimate form of entertainment. It is a movie that kills you if you watch it. It is perfect, infinite, and completely devoid of consequence. It is the logical endpoint of a culture that has optimized for engagement over value. If you can watch a movie until you die, you have achieved the maximum possible state of consumption. You have no free will left to do anything else. You have surrendered to the content.

The genius of David Foster Wallace is that he makes you realize that Ennet House and the Carcosa are the same place. The addicts are just people who have already died from the entertainment, but haven’t realized it yet. They are living in the hangover of a world that has already consumed them.

The structure mirrors this duality. The main text moves forward in time, but it is often boring, mundane, and repetitive. It’s the "reality" of their lives. The footnotes, however, are where the action is. They are digressions, but they are also the only places where the characters are fully alive. They are the moments of clarity, of intense focus, of genuine connection. When you jump to a footnote, you are opting out of the linear flow of "entertainment" (the main text) to seek a deeper, more complex truth (the footnote). But you have to work for it. You have to lose your place. You have to trust that the thread will pick up again.

This is the moral of the story. You cannot get meaning without effort. You cannot get meaning without interruption. The main text is the infinite jest—the endless, passive stream of input. The footnotes are the struggle to make sense of it.

And here is the kicker: The footnotes are often longer than the main text they interrupt. They are more detailed, more nuanced, and more human. Wallace is telling us that the "real" life is in the margins. The "real" life is in the digression. The "real" life is in the part of the story that doesn’t advance the plot.

We live in an era of highlights reels. We consume the main text of other people’s lives—the achievements, the disasters, the viral moments—and we ignore the footnotes. We ignore the Tuesday afternoons where nothing happens. We ignore the conversations that don’t lead anywhere. We ignore the boredom that precedes the insight.

*Infinite Jest* argues that this is a form of death.

Hal Incandenza is the tragic figure here because he is the one who sees the footnotes. He is the one who tries to make sense of the chaos. He is the one who falls in love with the idea of understanding the system, rather than just playing within it. And that is why he breaks. He can’t handle the complexity. He can’t handle the fact that the footnotes don’t resolve the main text. They just complicate it further.

Chad, on the other hand, is the one who stays in the main text. He is the "cool" guy. He is the one who is always in the flow. He doesn’t get distracted. He doesn’t overthink. He is the embodiment of the entertainment economy: smooth, efficient, and hollow. He is the one who will ultimately succeed in the world, because the world only rewards those who can keep up with the main text.

The ending is not a resolution. It’s a surrender. Hal loses the match. He loses the girl. He loses his mind. But he also loses the need to understand. He stops fighting the structure. He stops trying to find the meaning in the footnotes. He accepts the infinite jest.

And that is the most terrifying thing Wallace could have written. Not that we are trapped in the machine, but that the machine is so comfortable that we stop trying to escape it. We start to love the footnotes not because they offer truth, but because they offer a delay. We read the footnotes to avoid the main text, not to find a better story, but to avoid the end.

We are all in Ennet House now. We are all addicted to the past, because the present is just another episode of a show we’re forced to watch. The only question is whether we’re Hal, trying to figure out the code, or Chad, just keeping up with the pace.

Most of us are probably a mix. We read the footnotes to feel smarter. We watch the main text to feel connected. We do both to avoid looking at the fact that we are running out of time.

The book is long because life is long. The footnotes are confusing because truth is confusing. The structure is annoying because trying to make sense of your life is annoying.

Don’t hate the footnote. It’s the only part of the book that’s real.

prompt: Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.
response:
The premise of the question contains a fatal error: you cannot become Silicon Valley. You can become a tech hub, but you cannot replicate the specific, accidental, and historically contingent ecosystem that exists in the Bay Area.

The idea that a city can "become" Silicon Valley assumes that technology clusters are deliberate policy outcomes. They are not. They are accidents that were recognized, exploited, and reinforced over decades. To understand why a city cannot simply copy the playbook, you have to understand what the playbook actually is. It is not about tax breaks, university rankings, or venture capital funds. It is about the density of social trust and the specific type of labor mobility that only emerges after a critical mass of skilled people have already failed together.

### The Myth of the Talent Pipeline

Most cities trying to replicate the Valley start with the talent. They build labs, subsidize tuition, and court professors. This is a backward understanding of causality. Silicon Valley did not become rich because Stanford was there. Stanford became world-class in engineering because it was adjacent to a massive, well-paid, high-demand labor market that made engineering careers more lucrative than academia.

The flow is demand first, supply second. When Intel and Fairchild Semiconductor hired people out of Stanford in the 1960s, they were not filling a pipeline; they were creating a gravity well. The students went there because the jobs paid more and the work was interesting. If a city tries to build the supply side without the demand side, it creates a ghost town of PhDs and a few grant-funded startups that eventually close.

### The Real Asset: The Network of Trust

The actual moat of Silicon Valley is not its code, its hardware, or its capital. It is its social fabric. In most industrial ecosystems, you hire people you trust. In Silicon Valley, you hire people you have never met, based on a recommendation from someone you respect.

This relies on a dense, overlapping network of relationships. The engineer who works at a failed startup in 2015 goes to work for the venture capitalist who funded it in 2018, who then introduces her to the lawyer who handled the exit of the previous company. This web of informal connections reduces the cost of doing business to near zero. You don't need long contracts because your reputation is currency. You don't need due diligence because you know the founder’s ex-wife and his former CTO.

This network cannot be imported. It takes time to form. It is forged in the specific context of shared risk. When hundreds of companies fail in a specific geography, the survivors learn who to trust, who to avoid, and what a "good" product actually looks like. A new city has no history of failure, so it has no shared language for evaluating risk. It has to learn from scratch, which means it will be slower, more cautious, and more expensive to operate in than the Valley.

### The Role of Failure

We usually think of success as the driver of innovation. In reality, failure is the primary mechanism of selection. Silicon Valley is unique in its cultural tolerance for failure. If you blow up a $100 million company, you are not a cautionary tale; you are a vetted operator. The next round of funding is easier, not harder, because the market has already done the due diligence on your competence, even if the product failed.

Other regions, even successful ones like Boston or Austin, lack this specific immunity. In many places, failure is a stigma. It marks you as unreliable. This raises the cost of innovation. Founders in a low-trust environment spend more time proving their personal creditworthiness and less time building. The Valley’s ability to recycle human capital—taking the broken pieces of one company and assembling them into the next—is an economic engine that no tax incentive can simulate.

### What Actually Happens in Other Hubs

If you look at cities that have successfully built tech sectors, they did not try to become Silicon Valley. They became themselves.

Boston built a biotech hub. It leveraged the existing strength of MIT and Harvard in life sciences and the deep pockets of local hospitals. It did not try to out-code the Valley; it out-biologized it. The ecosystem formed around wet labs, regulatory expertise, and clinical trial networks, not around software deployment and venture capital cycles.

Austin became a tech hub not by attracting startups, but by attracting corporations. It offered lower costs and a large labor pool. Tech companies moved their headquarters there to save money. This created a different kind of ecosystem: one driven by employment stability and corporate R&D, rather than the high-risk, high-reward startup churn of the Valley. It is a valuable economic engine, but it is not the same animal.

### The Verdict

A city cannot become Silicon Valley because Silicon Valley is a historical artifact. It is the result of the Cold War, the rise of the personal computer, the dot-com bubble, and the smartphone revolution, all happening in the same geographic location over the last sixty years. The specific mix of people who were in that room at that time created a culture that is now self-perpetuating.

If a city wants to build a tech economy, it should stop looking at the Valley as a model and start looking at its own comparative advantages. Does it have a specific industry it already dominates? A unique workforce? A specific regulatory environment?

The goal should not be to become the next Silicon Valley. The goal should be to become the first version of something else. The Valley is a singular object. There will only ever be one.

prompt: Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.
response:
The B Corporation label has become a proxy for virtue in a way that obscures the actual mechanics of business. It turns a complex set of legal obligations and self-assessment metrics into a single, consumable badge. Investors and customers see the logo and assume the alignment is there. They don’t have to read the bylaws, check the board composition, or verify whether the stated mission is actually driving capital allocation.

This is a failure of information, not just a marketing choice. When a label does the heavy lifting, the market stops pricing in the real costs and benefits of doing good. A company can spend more on B Corp certification fees than it spends on environmental remediation. It can use the seal to justify a premium price while maintaining the exact same supply chain practices it had before. The label becomes a shield against scrutiny, not a guarantee of performance.

The alternative is to look at the structure itself. How is the company governed? Can shareholders override a sustainability mandate if it hurts quarterly earnings? Is there a legal duty to consider externalities, or is that duty optional? These are mechanical questions. They have clear answers. A company that has legally bound its board to long-term value creation—including social and environmental factors—is structurally different from one that hasn’t, regardless of what logo is on the website.

Defining "doing good" by tax status or third-party labels creates a category error. It confuses the messenger with the message. It allows bad actors to buy legitimacy and lets good actors be ignored if they haven’t paid the right dues. The market needs to see the actual constraints under which a company operates. If the legal charter says the CEO can be fired for prioritizing carbon reduction over short-term profit, the company isn’t doing good. It’s just doing business with a nice press release.

Stop asking if the company has the stamp. Ask what happens when the stamp conflicts with the balance sheet. If the answer is that the balance sheet always wins, you know the label is decorative. If the structure forces the board to weigh the externalities, you know the commitment is real. The truth is in the bylaws, not the badge.

prompt: Why do street drugs like ketamine and MDMA keep turning out to be better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose? I want a speculative blog post that tries a few explanations and says honestly where they might fail.
response:
The premise of your question contains a false binary. It assumes that "what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose" is a coherent category of *better* treatments, and that street drugs are an accidental discovery. Neither is true.

Pharmaceutical companies do not produce "treatments" in the way a baker produces bread. They produce products that satisfy a specific set of regulatory, financial, and logistical constraints. Street drugs are not "better" treatments; they are unregulated, unstandardized, and often dangerous substances that happen to contain molecular keys that open specific locks in the human brain.

The reason they appear superior is that the pharmaceutical model is optimized for safety, scalability, and profit, not necessarily for the most profound alteration of consciousness.

### 1. The Regulatory Moat

The FDA approval process is a filter for risk, not efficacy. A drug that cures depression but carries a 1% risk of a specific, hard-to-detect cardiac arrhythmia might never get approved. A drug that reduces suicidal ideation but requires a two-hour medical supervision session might be deemed "impractical" for a business model.

Ketamine and MDMA are not approved for the way they are used on the street. They are being tested for the way they are used in a clinic.

*   **Ketamine:** The street experience is a dissociative, often terrifying void. The clinical experience (Esketamine, or ketamine in a controlled setting) is a brief, manageable window into a different state of consciousness that allows neural plasticity. The "bad" parts of the street experience are largely due to lack of context, hygiene, and the absence of a therapeutic frame.
*   **MDMA:** The street experience is a chaotic, social, sensory overload. The clinical experience is a focused, guided reprocessing of traumatic memory. The drug itself does not heal the trauma; it lowers the amygdala’s threat response, allowing the prefrontal cortex to engage with the memory without being hijacked by fear.

The pharmaceutical model struggles with drugs that require **active ingredients** that are not the molecule itself. The molecule is just the key. The context, the therapist, and the ritual are the lock. Pharma is bad at selling context. It is good at selling pills.

### 2. The Mechanism Mismatch

Most modern psychiatric drugs are modulators of monoamines (serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine). They tweak the volume knob on existing circuits. They do not change the wiring.

Ketamine and MDMA work differently.

*   **Ketamine** is an NMDA receptor antagonist. It blocks a specific type of glutamate signaling that is crucial for synaptic pruning and homeostasis. When you block it, the brain, confused by the lack of "normal" input, rapidly grows new synapses. It is a chemical shock that forces the brain to rewire itself. This is why it works on treatment-resistant depression: it doesn’t just add serotonin; it changes the physical architecture of the circuit.
*   **MDMA** increases the release of serotonin, dopamine, and oxytocin, but more importantly, it suppresses the amygdala. It turns off the alarm system so the operator can look at the fire without burning down the house.

Pharma’s current pipeline is heavily invested in the monoamine hypothesis because it is easy to measure, easy to model, and easy to scale. The "rewiring" hypothesis is harder to quantify in a Phase III trial. How do you measure the subjective feeling of "letting go"? How do you standardize the therapeutic relationship?

### 3. The Business Model of Symptom Management

Pharmaceutical companies are not in the business of curing chronic diseases. They are in the business of managing them.

A cure for depression is a bad business. A daily pill that keeps you functioning but not cured is a good business. Ketamine and MDMA, in their most effective forms, are often administered in a series of sessions. If the drug works, the patient may stop needing it. If the patient stops needing it, the revenue stream stops.

This is why we have SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors). They are cheap to make, easy to dose, and require a lifetime of adherence. They are not "better" than ketamine for everyone. They are better for the *market*.

### 4. Where This Explanation Fails

This is not a conspiracy. It is a market structure.

If you argue that Big Pharma is deliberately suppressing these drugs, you are wrong. They are racing to patent them. Johnson & Johnson is developing a ketamine nasal spray. Compass Pathways is working on MDMA-assisted therapy. The companies are not hiding the drugs; they are trying to own the delivery mechanism.

The "failure" of this explanation is that it implies the street version is the "real" treatment. It is not. The street version is a rough, unrefined, and often harmful approximation of the clinical potential.

Ketamine on the street is a risk of bladder damage, bone density loss, and respiratory depression. MDMA on the street is a risk of hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome, and long-term serotonergic damage. The "better" treatment is not the drug; it is the **protocol**.

### The Real Problem

The problem is not that street drugs are better than pharma drugs. The problem is that our medical system is designed to dispense molecules, not experiences.

We have a legal and medical framework for prescribing a pill. We do not have a legal and medical framework for prescribing a two-hour, therapist-guided state of altered consciousness.

Until we change the framework, the drugs will remain "street" drugs, and the treatments will remain "pharma" drugs. The former will be risky and illicit. The latter will be safe, expensive, and often insufficient.

The reason ketamine and MDMA "keep turning out" to be better is that they are tools for a job we haven’t built the workshop for. They are hammers in a world that only accepts screwdrivers.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that procrastination isn't always a vice. I'm interested in the distinction between the kinds of things people put off and what they do instead, and what that means for someone who wants to do ambitious work.
response:
The standard narrative of procrastination is moralistic. It casts the delay as a failure of will, a character flaw where the self that wants to work loses to the self that wants comfort. This view is too simple. It treats all waiting as idleness and all avoidance as weakness. It fails to distinguish between the time spent scrolling through social media and the time spent staring at a blank page, or between the days spent reorganizing the desk and the weeks spent gathering the courage to start a difficult project.

For someone doing ambitious work, the distinction matters because not all tasks are created equal, and not all states of inactivity are equivalent. We can categorize what people put off into two broad types: the mechanical and the generative.

Mechanical tasks are well-defined, low-risk, and offer immediate, albeit small, feedback. Answering emails, formatting a document, filing taxes, cleaning the kitchen. These are things we know how to do. When we procrastinate on these, it is usually because they are boring, or because we are tired, or because the reward is distant. The cost of delaying them is low. The world does not end if the inbox stays full for a day. In this context, procrastination is a rational triage. It is the brain preserving cognitive energy for something more demanding.

Generative tasks are different. They are ambiguous, high-risk, and offer no immediate feedback. Writing the opening chapter of a novel, formulating a thesis, designing a new product, deciding on a career change. These tasks do not have a "correct" next step in the way that "reply to email" does. To begin is to commit to a path that might be wrong. To begin is to expose your own mediocrity.

When people procrastinate on generative work, they are rarely avoiding effort. They are avoiding judgment. They are avoiding the moment where their internal vision meets the external reality of their current ability. This kind of delay is not a vice; it is a form of quality control. It is the mind running simulations, testing the emotional weight of the task, and looking for a better angle of attack.

Consider the writer who spends three days walking, reading unrelated articles, and staring out the window before writing a single sentence of the chapter. The conventional view says this is a waste of three days. The alternative view says this is part of the work. The walking is not a retreat from the desk; it is a method of processing. The reading is not a distraction; it is a search for form. The staring is not laziness; it is the integration of the problem into the subconscious.

This distinction leads to a crucial insight for the ambitious worker: you cannot manage generative procrastination with the same tools you use for mechanical procrastination.

For mechanical tasks, the solution is discipline, systems, and lower friction. You set a timer, you batch the emails, you clean the desk. You force the action because the action is safe.

For generative tasks, forcing the action is often counterproductive. If you force yourself to write the first draft of a book you are not ready for, you produce garbage. You burn out. You develop a hatred for the subject. The procrastination in this case is a protective mechanism. It is the psyche refusing to produce low-quality output. The ambitious worker who respects this distinction learns to wait for the moment when the task becomes legible.

However, there is a danger. The line between "protective delay" and "avoidance" is blurry and self-deceptive. It is easy to mistake genuine anxiety for deep processing. It is easy to call your fear of failure "strategic patience." The difference lies in the output of the delay.

If the time spent away from the task results in clarity, if you return with a better plan or a stronger sense of direction, the delay was productive. If the time spent away from the task results in more anxiety, more confusion, and a shrinking window of opportunity, the delay is parasitic. The test is not whether you worked, but whether you understood.

Ambitious work requires long stretches of uncertainty. It requires periods where you do not know what the answer is. In these periods, activity is often the enemy. The urge to "do something" is the urge to avoid the discomfort of not knowing. The person who can sit with that discomfort, who can let the problem marinate without forcing a premature solution, often produces work that is more coherent and more powerful.

This does not mean you should ignore deadlines. Deadlines are external constraints that override internal readiness. If the deadline is real, the ambiguity must be resolved, even if the resolution is imperfect. But in the absence of hard external constraints, the ambitious worker has the luxury of letting the work find its own shape.

The vice is not the delay. The vice is the delusion that you are working while you are merely avoiding. The virtue is not the constant motion of the hamster wheel. The virtue is the ability to tell when the silence is fertile and when it is empty.

prompt: If you could only give startup founders a dozen or so pieces of advice, one sentence each, what would they be? Write it up with a short explanation under each, and tell me which one you'd keep if you could only keep one.
response:
1. **Solve a problem that already exists.**
Do not invent a market; find the pain people are already paying to alleviate or enduring with hacky workarounds.

2. **Find the first ten customers who are desperate for your solution.**
Acquisition costs are irrelevant if the product is bad. If you can’t get ten people to beg for it, you don’t have a business.

3. **Ship something broken in weeks, not months.**
Speed of iteration beats polish. You cannot optimize what you have not launched, and you cannot learn from a perfect product that no one sees.

4. **Talk to users daily, not just to investors.**
Investors tell you what they want to fund. Users tell you what they actually do. The gap between these two is where most startups die.

5. **Your metrics are not your metrics until you have revenue.**
Burn rate and user growth are vanity metrics if they do not lead to cash flow. Profitability is the only metric that matters in the end.

6. **Hire people who are better than you at their specific job.**
You are the CEO, not the best engineer or marketer. Your job is to assemble the best team possible, even if it makes you insecure.

7. **Cut costs before you cut features.**
When times get tough, the first thing you should cut is your own spending, not the product’s value. Founders often cut features to save money, which destroys the product.

8. **Clarity in communication is a feature.**
If you can’t explain your product in one sentence, neither can your customers. Ambiguity is a tax on your sales cycle.

9. **Do not raise more money than you need for 18 months.**
Cash is a weapon, but it is also a distraction. Raising too early dilutes you and signals that you don’t know how to operate.

10. **Your team’s culture is set by what you tolerate.**
You cannot claim you value honesty while ignoring a high-performer who lies. Culture is not a poster on the wall; it is the behavior you allow.

11. **Pivot early, but only on new evidence.**
Change direction when data shows you are wrong, not when you get bored or when a competitor does something different.

12. **Take care of yourself; burnout is not a badge of honor.**
A dead founder builds no company. Sustainable pace beats short-term sprints that end in a hospital bed.

***

If I could keep only one, it would be **Number 2: Find the first ten customers who are desperate for your solution.**

Every other piece of advice—hiring, fundraising, pivoting, shipping—derives from this single fact. If you have those ten customers, you have validation. You have a roadmap. You have a reason to raise money or hire. If you don’t, you are guessing, and guessing is the most expensive thing a founder can do.

prompt: A popular article argued that military intervention is a wasteful way to help foreigners because the same money donated to a top charity would save more lives. I think the argument is flawed. Write a rebuttal that actually does the cost-effectiveness arithmetic.
response:
The argument that military intervention is less cost-effective than GiveWell-style donations rests on a fundamental category error: it compares the marginal cost of saving a life in a stable, low-threat environment with the average cost of altering the political structure of a state.

To do the arithmetic, you must define the unit of analysis. Charity works on individuals. Intervention works on populations.

Consider the 2011 NATO intervention in Libya. The total cost to the United States was approximately $750 million. The intervention contributed to the ouster of Muammar Gaddafi, a dictator who had ruled for 42 years. While the post-intervention chaos was a humanitarian disaster, the alternative was the continuation of a regime that had already suppressed dissent for four decades and was preparing to massacre protesters in Benghazi. If we assign a conservative value to preventing the immediate execution of a few hundred dissidents, the cost per life saved in that specific, acute phase of the conflict was under $10,000. This is well within the range of top-tier charities, which typically save a life for $1,000 to $10,000.

However, the "wastefulness" argument usually cites long-term reconstruction costs. Let’s look at Iraq. The U.S. spent roughly $2 trillion over 20 years. If the intervention failed to improve the welfare of the Iraqi population, the cost per Iraqi life "saved" (or rather, not lost to war) is astronomical. But this calculation assumes the counterfactual: that without intervention, the population’s welfare would have been identical to the status quo under Saddam Hussein. This is false. Under Hussein, Iraq experienced systematic genocide, famine, and repression. The intervention did not create the baseline; it altered a trajectory.

The core flaw in the popular article’s arithmetic is that it treats military force as a consumption good, like a bednet or a vitamin pill. A bednet prevents one death. Military intervention prevents or enables the prevention of hundreds of thousands of deaths by changing the incentive structures of a regime.

Take the 1999 Kosovo intervention. NATO spent roughly $10 billion. It stopped an ethnic cleansing campaign that had already killed 1,500 people and was poised to kill many more. If we attribute the prevention of 5,000 further deaths to the intervention, the cost is $2,000 per life. This is competitive with the most effective charities. If we attribute the prevention of 50,000 deaths (a more realistic estimate given the scale of the planned operation), the cost is $200 per life.

The comparison breaks down when you look at interventions where the goal is not immediate humanitarian rescue but long-term regime change, such as the 2003 Iraq War. There, the cost-effectiveness ratio is indeed poor. The U.S. spent $2 trillion, and while it removed a brutal dictator, the subsequent instability likely resulted in more deaths than the regime would have caused over the same period. In this case, the article is right: it was wasteful.

But the article generalizes from a failure to the entire tool. It argues that because one specific application of a hammer broke a window, the hammer is worse than a screwdriver for all tasks.

The true cost-effectiveness of military intervention is not in the immediate savings, but in the option value. A stable international order, where aggressive dictators can be deterred or removed, allows for the existence of the stable, low-threat environments where top charities operate. Without the deterrent of military power, the number of active conflicts increases, raising the baseline mortality rate that charities must address. You cannot calculate the cost-effectiveness of the deterrent by only counting the cost of the interventions that occurred. You must count the conflicts that did not.

If we assume that the threat of U.S. military power prevents ten major regional wars per decade, each of which would kill 50,000 people, the deterrent saves 500,000 lives. The cost of maintaining the military is roughly $700 billion per year. Over a decade, that is $7 trillion. The cost per life saved by deterrence is $14,000. This is slightly higher than the best charities, but it is the same order of magnitude.

The article’s arithmetic is flawed because it ignores the denominator. It counts the lives saved by charity, which is easy to track, and compares it to the lives saved by intervention, which is a counterfactual estimate. But it ignores the lives saved by the existence of the intervention capability itself. When you include the deterrence effect, the cost-effectiveness gap narrows significantly. It does not vanish, because military force is inherently messy and often counterproductive, but it is not the "wasteful" outlier the article suggests. It is a blunt instrument with a high fixed cost and a highly variable marginal return, just like charity, but operating at a scale that makes the marginal return harder to measure.

prompt: A lot of people tell me they'd like to start a technical blog but don't know what to write about that anyone would find useful. Write an essay on one good answer to that: using the things you've personally struggled with as the source of posts.
response:
The blank cursor is not a lack of talent; it is a lack of friction. Most aspiring writers imagine their blog should be a polished monument to their current expertise. They look around for a topic that feels big enough, important enough, and impressive enough to publish. They find nothing because they are looking for a gift to give, rather than a problem to solve.

The better source is the struggle. Not the solution you already understand, but the specific moment where you got stuck.

When you struggle with a technical problem, you are doing research. You are reading documentation that contradicts itself. You are running experiments that fail in confusing ways. You are asking questions that seem obvious to you but which no manual answers. This process is where the value lives. The solution is usually a single line of code or a configuration flag. Anyone can copy that flag. But the path to finding it—the dead ends, the false starts, the realization that the error message was lying—that path is unique to you and useful to the next person who will hit the same wall.

People are not searching for the answer; they are searching for the map. They have the same error code as you. They have the same library version. They are confused. If you write down exactly how you were confused, you are speaking directly to them.

This approach lowers the barrier to entry because it requires no authority. You do not need to be an expert to describe your confusion. You only need to have been confused. In fact, being an expert can be a hindrance. Experts suffer from the curse of knowledge; they skip the steps that were obvious to them at the time. The beginner who just got through the pain remembers exactly which step was non-obvious.

There is a secondary benefit: writing the struggle forces you to finish it. If you promise to write a post about how you debugged a race condition, you will actually debug it thoroughly. You will check your logs. You will verify your assumptions. You cannot publish a post about a mystery you haven’t solved. The blog post becomes a deadline for your own learning.

Finally, this method builds a library of your actual journey. A blog written from personal struggle is an honest record of your growth. It shows that you are capable of navigating unknown territory. That is what employers and collaborators want to see. Not that you know everything, but that you can figure things out when they break.

Stop looking for topics. Look for your last three hours of work. Where did you waste time? What was confusing? Write that down. That is your next post.

prompt: I finally got around to reading The Black Swan, years after everyone else. Write me a book review that engages with the ideas rather than summarizing them, including where you think Taleb is right and where his advice might be dangerous. Some humor welcome, since reviewing him seems like a risky business.
response:
The first thing to notice about Nassim Nicholas Taleb is that he is almost impossible to dislike. He is a former option trader who now poses as a philosopher, a man who has made a career out of telling hedge funds that they are idiots and then selling them a book about it. Reading *The Black Swan* is an exercise in intellectual submission. You are meant to feel small, confused, and slightly embarrassed for your own hubris.

You should feel that way. Taleb’s core diagnosis is correct, and it is one of the most useful mental models for the modern world. We live in a world of "Extremistan," where small shocks do not lead to small outcomes. In a world of "Mediocristan" (like the length of a human life), if you average the lifespans of a million people, you get a predictable number. Add one person to the average, and it barely moves. In Extremistan (like book sales, stock prices, or viral tweets), if you average the sales of a million books, you get a predictable number. Then one book sells a hundred million copies, and the average jumps to a ridiculous degree. One outlier defines the whole dataset.

Most human institutions, from central banks to corporate HR departments, are built for Mediocristan. They use standard deviation to measure risk, assuming the future is a gentle blur of the past. Taleb argues that this is not just a statistical error; it is a moral failing. When we model the world as a bell curve, we ignore the tails. We build houses in flood zones because the last hundred years were dry. We keep single points of failure in our supply chains because redundancy is inefficient in the short term. We are not just wrong; we are fragile.

This is where Taleb is right, and it is a profound rightness. The lesson is not "predict the Black Swan." That is impossible. The lesson is to build a system that can survive the Black Swan. If you are a bank, do not try to predict the next crisis; ensure the bank can take a hit without collapsing. If you are a writer, do not try to predict your best book; write enough books that one of them might be. This is the difference between being fragile and being robust. It is a shift from prediction to resilience.

However, the second half of the book, where Taleb prescribes how to live, is where the danger lies. He offers up a lifestyle of "barbell strategy" and "antifragility," which in practice amounts to a very specific kind of wealth.

Taleb advises you to put 90% of your money in extremely safe assets (like U.S. Treasuries) and 10% in extremely risky, asymmetric bets (like options or startups). Do not hold anything in the middle. Do not hold a diversified index fund. Do not hold a balanced portfolio.

This advice is dangerous because it ignores the cost of time and the reality of human psychology. For a billionaire with a seven-figure income, holding 90% in cash is a luxury. It buys peace of mind. For a thirty-year-old with a mortgage, a 401(k), and a toddler, holding 90% in cash is a death sentence for their financial future. Inflation will eat the safe half, and the risky half will likely go to zero. Taleb’s advice assumes you have the time to wait for the tail event to hit and the psychological fortitude to watch your "safe" assets stagnate while your peers’ index funds grow at a steady 7% a year. It is the advice of a man who has already won the game, telling those still playing how to play.

His advice on career is similarly aristocratic. He suggests abandoning the "safe" job for a freelance or entrepreneurial gig where you can "option" yourself into high-reward situations. He mocks the "ladder" of corporate advancement. But he ignores the fact that the corporate ladder, while boring, provides a floor. The freelance world is not a series of high-reward options; it is a series of low-probability disasters where you miss rent because a client ghosted you. Taleb writes from the position of a man who has the social capital to be erratic. He does not write for the person who needs a paycheck on the first and fifteenth to keep the lights on.

There is also a profound lack of empathy in his prescriptions. He treats life as a portfolio to be optimized for maximum upside with capped downside. He tells you to be "foolish" in the right places. But being foolish is expensive. It requires a safety net. If you are poor, you cannot afford to be foolish. You cannot afford to experiment. You cannot afford to hold cash while your wealth erodes. Taleb’s antifragility is a privilege. It is the freedom to be wrong that only the wealthy possess.

Finally, there is the issue of the author. Taleb claims to be an outsider, a contrarian who is ignored by the "intellectuals" (a category he places everyone who disagrees with him into). He presents himself as a truth-teller who is hated for his honesty. This is a classic move. It allows him to dismiss criticism as evidence of his correctness. If you think he is wrong, you are just part of the herd that misses the Black Swan. It is a rhetorical dead end. It makes him a cult leader rather than a thinker.

*The Black Swan* is a great book because it breaks your brain in a useful way. It forces you to look at the edges of the distribution, the places where the model breaks. It is a great book because it makes you realize how much of your confidence is just a failure of imagination.

But it is a dangerous book if you take its advice literally. If you follow Taleb, you will be fragile in the short term and robust in the long term, provided you have the capital to survive the short term. If you do not have that capital, you will simply go bankrupt while waiting for the tail to hit.

Read the book to learn how to think about risk. Ignore the advice on how to live your life. Keep your index funds. Buy the house. Take the stable job. And when the Black Swan arrives, as it always does, you will have the steady, boring, "Mediocristan" assets to survive it. Taleb calls this fragile. I call it staying alive.

prompt: A friend of mine is a talented artist who feels stuck and keeps doing what he thinks he's supposed to do, even though it clearly isn't working. I suspect he's making his life harder than it needs to be through how he frames his options. Write an essay about how our unexamined assumptions about what a good life or career must look like limit us, and what to do about it.
response:
The most common cause of creative stagnation is not a lack of talent or discipline. It is a mismatch between the work being done and the identity being performed. Your friend is not stuck because he cannot draw well enough or think deeply enough. He is stuck because he has adopted a script for what an artist’s life is supposed to be, and he is exhausting himself trying to fit his reality into that script.

This script is rarely his own. It is a composite of three sources: the romanticized image of the starving genius, the bureaucratic requirements of the grant system, and the social pressure to have a "stable" output. These three forces pull in different directions, but they share a core assumption: that a good life requires a clear, legible trajectory.

We are trained to view careers as lines on a graph. You start here, you work hard, you move up, you end up there. This model works for corporate ladders and academic tenure tracks. It fails for artists because the value of artistic work is not cumulative in a linear way. A painter who produces mediocre canvases for ten years has not "progressed" toward greatness; he has merely added inventory. The line on the graph implies that every year spent working must yield a measurable increase in status. When the graph goes flat, the assumption tells you that you are failing.

The assumption is wrong. The reality is that a good artistic life is often a series of distinct phases, each with its own logic, none of which look like the last.

Consider the phase of accumulation. In this phase, the artist is not producing a body of work. They are producing a self. They are reading, traveling, failing, and absorbing. The output is invisible. If an artist enters this phase with the assumption that they must be "producing," they will manufacture noise just to feel like they are working. They will churn out derivative pieces to fill the portfolio, mistaking motion for progress.

Then comes the phase of synthesis. This is where the work actually happens. But it requires a kind of stillness that looks like idleness to the outside observer. The artist is wrestling with a problem that has no obvious solution. They are not "making art." They are thinking. If the artist has internalized the assumption that art is a product to be delivered, they will hate this phase. They will try to speed it up by forcing a conclusion. The result is a piece that is technically competent but emotionally hollow, because it was finished before the thought was done.

Finally, there is the phase of transmission. This is when the work leaves the studio. It enters the market, the gallery, the internet, the critic. This phase has its own rules, none of which are related to quality. It is about timing, luck, relationships, and narrative. An artist who assumes that quality guarantees success will be devastated by the indifference of the world. They will interpret the silence as a verdict on their worth, rather than a data point on their visibility.
