Your friend is stuck because he is trying to apply the rules of one phase to another. He is in the synthesis phase, but he is measuring himself by the metrics of the transmission phase. He sees that no one is buying his work, so he concludes he is not making good work. Or he is in the accumulation phase, but he is measuring himself by the metrics of the synthesis phase. He feels empty, so he thinks he has run out of ideas.

The assumption that limits us is the belief that we must know where we are on the graph at all times. It creates a feedback loop of anxiety. Because we do not have a clear metric for success in the current moment, we feel unsafe. Because we feel unsafe, we retreat to the only thing that feels safe: the routine. We do what we have always done because it is familiar, even though it is not working.

To break this, the artist must decouple their identity from their output. This is a psychological skill, not an artistic one. It requires admitting that the current activity is not the final form of the life.

Practically, this means stopping the search for the "right" project and starting the search for the right constraint.

If the artist feels stuck, the problem is usually that the options are too large. "Make art" is a void. It contains every possible thing, which means it contains nothing. The artist needs a constraint that is small enough to execute but large enough to force a decision.

A constraint might be: "I will only use black and white for the next month." Or: "I will make a piece that fits in my pocket." Or: "I will spend three weeks doing nothing but visiting places I have never been, with no sketchbook."

The value of the constraint is that it removes the need to judge the work while it is being made. The artist does not have to decide if the black-and-white drawing is "good." They only have to decide if it is black and white. The judgment comes later, when the piece is done. By the time the piece is done, the artist has moved on to the next problem.

This approach respects the nature of the work. It treats the process as a way of thinking, not a way of performing. It allows the artist to be a beginner again, which is the only state from which new things can be made.

The friend is not a failure. He is a person with a set of tools and a set of assumptions that do not match. The tools are fine. The assumptions are the obstacle. He does not need to be more talented. He needs to be less sure.

prompt: You've been running a small software business that sells to teachers for a few years, mostly in spare hours around a brutal Japanese salaryman job, and you're about to quit to go full time. Write a long, practical blog post for programmers who want to run a business on the side with only a few hours a week: what actually lets you pull it off?
response:
The graveyard of side-hustle programming is full of ambitious people who died of exhaustion, not failure. They had a good idea. They wrote clean code. They lost because they tried to run a company with four hours a week of sleep-deprived attention.

I spent five years selling software to middle school teachers in Japan while working a 60-hour week at a systems integrator. I quit last month. I’m writing this because the transition from "side project" to "full-time business" is not a vertical scale-up. It’s a horizontal shift in what your hours actually do.

If you have a day job, your time is not continuous. It is fragmented. It is 7:00 AM to 8:30 AM on a Tuesday, and 10:00 PM to midnight on a Friday. It is not a 40-hour block. You cannot build a business that requires continuous momentum. You have to build a business that runs on inertia and batch processing.

Here is what actually lets you pull it off.

### 1. Sell the shovel, not the gold

When you have limited hours, you cannot afford to iterate on a product that users have to figure out. If your software requires a 30-minute onboarding video, you are dead. You have no time to support them. You have no time to fix the confusion.

Your product must be so simple that the "how to" is obvious. In my case, I built a gradebook plugin for a specific LMS (Learning Management System). Teachers don’t want to "manage student data workflows." They want to stop copying numbers from a spreadsheet into a database. The interface was three buttons. That simplicity was the only reason I could support 200 schools without hiring anyone.

Complexity is expensive. Every feature you add is a future support ticket. Every support ticket is an hour you don’t have. If you can’t answer an email in 10 minutes, your product is too complex.

### 2. Automate the boring stuff until it hurts

You are going to have days where you are too tired to think. You will have meetings at 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM. The middle of the day is yours, but it is often broken up by errands, commutes, and the mental hangover of your day job.

You need a system that works when you are absent. This means:
*   **Self-serve billing.** No invoicing. No chasing payments. Stripe, Paddle, or similar. If a teacher has to email you to get a receipt, you have failed.
*   **Automated onboarding.** The moment they pay, they get access. No "I’ll send you the credentials tomorrow."
*   **Passive support.** A FAQ that actually answers questions. I wrote my FAQ by reading every email I got for six months. If a question appears three times, it goes in the FAQ. If the FAQ works, your support volume drops by 40%.

You are not building a startup. You are building a vending machine. It has to dispense the product without your intervention.

### 3. Pick a niche so narrow it feels embarrassing

Generalists lose. If you sell to "education," you are fighting for attention against LTI vendors with marketing budgets. If you sell to "math teachers in public schools in Ohio," you win.

Why? Because trust travels in small groups. Teachers talk. If one math teacher in Cleveland likes your tool, she tells the other math teachers in Cleveland. They tell the math teachers in the district. You don’t need a marketing team. You need one champion.

When you go narrow, your marketing is just being present where they already are. For me, that was a few Twitter chats and a subreddit. I didn’t write blog posts. I didn’t run ads. I answered questions. When I answered a question, I included a link to my tool only if it was directly relevant. It felt like help, not sales.

### 4. The "Two-Week Rule" for scope

You will have ideas. You will look at your code and think, "If I just add this feature, they’ll love it more."

Do not do it.

You have a day job. You have a life. You have a limit on how much you can sustain. Use the two-week rule: If a feature doesn’t solve a problem that is causing a customer to churn or a prospect to not buy, it is a waste.

I wanted to add a graphing feature for student progress. I spent three weeks building it. I showed it to ten teachers. Eight said, "Cool, but I don’t have time to look at graphs during the school day." Two said, "Nice."

I deleted the code. I kept the revenue. The graphing feature was a vanity project disguised as a product improvement. It cost me three weeks of sleep.

### 5. Financial clarity is a mental health tool

You need to know your break-even point. Not your "profit" point. Your break-even.

How many licenses do I need to sell to cover my server costs, my software subscriptions, and my taxes? For me, it was 14 licenses.

This number is your anchor. On the nights when you are working on a bug at 11:00 PM and your boss is on the phone with you about a deadline for Monday, you look at that number. If you have 14, you are safe. If you have 15, you are making money.

This removes the anxiety of "Is this working?" It becomes a binary check. You are either above the line or below it. You don’t need to guess.

### 6. Protect your day job like a fortress

You need the salary to fund the risk. You cannot afford to be fired, or to have your performance slip, because the side project is "on your mind."

This means:
*   **No side-project talk at work.** Not even to friends. If HR finds out you are running a competing or even a non-competing business, you are a liability.
*   **Use personal devices for business.** Do not use your company laptop to send invoices. Do not use your company Wi-Fi to log into your Stripe dashboard. It is not about legality; it is about psychology. You need a wall between the two identities.
*   **Be reliable at your day job.** If your side project causes you to miss a deadline at your day job, you have lost. You can miss a deadline at your side project. You cannot miss one at your day job.

### 7. The exit strategy is the start strategy

You are going to quit. You need to know when.

I decided I would quit when I had six months of expenses in the bank, and when my side income had been above my day-job income for three consecutive months.

This is not a vague goal. This is a checklist.
1.  Bank balance: $40,000.
2.  MRR: $8,000.
3.  Timeframe: Three months.

I hit this in October. I gave two weeks’ notice in November.

If you don’t have a specific number, you will never quit. You will keep working the day job because the side business is "almost" enough. "Almost" is a place where you live, not a place where you go.

### The reality of the grind

There are no magic hacks. The reason this works is that it is boring. It is repetitive. It is selling the same simple thing to the same small group of people.

Programmers are drawn to complexity. We want to build the next big platform. We want to use the latest framework. We want to scale to millions of users.

But you don’t have the hours for that. You have the hours for a small, steady, reliable business.

If you can accept that you will be small, you can afford to be free. If you need to be big, you should stay at your day job and invest in index funds. It is less fun, but it will not burn you out.

Start small. Sell one thing. Keep your day job. Save the money. Then leave.

prompt: I'm in the second year of a PhD and keep hearing that what separates good researchers is 'research taste', the ability to pick good problems. Nobody tells you how to actually get better at it. Can you write something practical on how to deliberately develop research taste, including the common ways people go wrong?
response:
Research taste is not a mystical sixth sense. It is pattern recognition built on a specific kind of exposure. Most second-year PhD students lack taste because they have consumed too many results and too few failures.

To develop it, you must change what you read and how you read it.

### Consume the negative space

The standard advice is to read recent high-impact papers. This is bad advice for developing taste. High-impact papers show you what works. They hide the landscape of what was tried, what was close, and why it failed.

Start reading the negative results in your field. Look for "we tried X, it didn't work, here is why" sections. Look for rebuttals at conferences like NeurIPS or ICML. Look for preprint servers where authors post work that didn't quite make the cut. When you read a rejection letter or a reviewer comment, you are seeing the exact criteria that separate a good problem from a bad one. You are seeing the boundary line.

### The "So What?" Test

A common failure mode is solving a hard mathematical problem that no one cares about. You spend two years proving a lemma that tightens a bound by 0.0001. It is rigorous. It is correct. It is boring.

When evaluating a problem, ask: "If I solve this, who is relieved?" If the answer is "only me," drop it. If the answer is "my advisor," keep it, but know it is a stepping stone, not a destination. If the answer is "the whole subfield," you have a good problem.

Good problems are bottlenecks. They are things that block other people from doing their work. If you remove the bottleneck, you unblock a lot of research. That is value.

### Avoid the "New Toy" Trap

Another failure mode is picking a problem because it allows you to use a new method. "I want to apply graph neural networks to this." This is not a problem; it is a tool. Tools are interchangeable. Problems are not.

Invert the question. Do not ask, "What can I apply GNNs to?" Ask, "Where is the current structure of the data causing existing methods to fail?" If the answer is "nowhere," do not use GNNs. If the answer is "the current methods assume Euclidean space, but the data is a manifold," then you have a problem. The method is just the answer to the problem, not the problem itself.

### Calibrate with Small Failures

Taste is a calibration of effort. You need to know how long a "medium" difficulty problem takes. If you have only ever done easy assignments, you will underestimate the time required for a hard problem by a factor of ten.

Run small projects on the side. Pick a problem that seems solvable in two weeks. Try to solve it. If it takes two months, your calibration is off. Do this repeatedly. After five of these small failures, you will develop a gut feeling for the scope of a problem. You will see a paper and know, "That claim looks too easy," or "That proof looks impossible."

### Watch the Advisors, Not the Papers

Look at who the successful researchers in your field are advising. What kinds of students do they take? What are the common threads in their recent papers?

If a lab publishes a paper on "Robust Optimization for Supply Chains," and then their next paper is "Robust Optimization for Healthcare," and then "Robust Optimization for Energy," they have a method. They are not driven by problems. They are driven by a technique they want to sell.

If a lab publishes "Quantum Error Correction," then "Quantum Simulation," then "Quantum Algorithms," they are driven by the domain.

You want to work in a problem-driven environment. But you also need to know where the money and the attention are. Taste includes knowing which problems are currently unfashionable but will become fashionable in three years. That is a timing skill, not a truth skill.

### The Practical Routine

1.  **Read the "Rejected" pile.** Find a conference in your field. Look at the papers that were rejected last year but are still cited. Why did they fail? What was missing?
2.  **The One-Paragraph Pitch.** Write a one-paragraph description of your potential PhD thesis. Show it to three people who are not in your lab. If they ask "why should I care?" you have a problem. If they ask "how would you do that?" you have a problem. If they ask "what is this?" you have a communication problem. Fix the communication first.
3.  **Kill your pet ideas fast.** If you cannot explain why your idea is hard in one sentence, it is not hard. If you cannot explain why it is useful in one sentence, it is not useful. Do not spend six months on an idea you cannot defend in one minute.

Taste is not about being original. It is about being right about what matters. You get better by seeing more of the landscape, especially the parts that are broken.

prompt: An economist I read argues that psychiatric illnesses like alcoholism, ADHD and schizophrenia are best understood as unusual preferences rather than diseases, since they don't look like the 'budget constraints' that physical illnesses are. You're a practicing psychiatrist. Write a thorough reply explaining where that argument goes wrong.
response:
The argument rests on a category error that confuses the mechanism of injury with the manifestation of behavior. To say a person with schizophrenia has an "unusual preference" for hearing voices is no more accurate than saying a person with a fractured femur has an unusual preference for dragging their leg. In both cases, the individual’s behavior is constrained by a physical reality that limits their options, but the nature of that constraint is entirely different.

In economics, a budget constraint is external. It is the price of butter or the number of hours in a day. It does not change based on the subject’s internal state. In psychiatry, the "constraint" is endogenous and biological. It is a malfunctioning of the system itself.

Take ADHD. The economist sees a lack of focus and labels it a preference for distraction. This ignores the neurobiology of the prefrontal cortex and the dopaminergic pathways. A child with ADHD does not choose to fail to inhibit impulses; the hardware responsible for inhibition is underactive. You cannot "budget" your way out of a neural deficit any more than you can budget your way out of a missing kidney. The cost of "curing" the preference would be the same as the cost of "curing" the disease: significant pharmacological intervention, which acts on the same chemical systems as the pathology. If the cause is biological, the label is disease.

Schizophrenia makes the error even more glaring. The argument requires that the delusion is a rational choice made by an agent with stable preferences. But the agent is not stable. The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia describes a state where the brain’s salience attribution system is broken. The patient hears voices because the neural networks that distinguish self-generated thoughts from external stimuli have failed. This is not a preference for auditory hallucinations; it is a failure of signal processing. To call it a preference is to engage in a form of moralistic reductio ad absurdum. It shifts the burden of the pathology onto the victim, implying they are simply choosing a difficult life over an easy one, when in fact they are trapped in a biological prison.

Alcoholism is the most difficult case because it begins with a choice. No one is born addicted. However, the transition from choice to compulsion is the definition of the disease. The "unusual preference" argument fails to account for the plasticity of the brain. Chronic exposure to alcohol rewires the reward circuitry. The amygdala and prefrontal cortex are altered. The "preference" becomes an imperative driven by neuroadaptations that the individual did not choose and cannot easily reverse. The economist looks at the current behavior and sees a preference for alcohol. The psychiatrist looks at the history and sees a progressive loss of control due to structural change in the brain.

Finally, the distinction matters for treatment. If these are preferences, the solution is moral exhortation or economic incentives. If they are diseases, the solution is medical intervention. We treat schizophrenia with antipsychotics that block dopamine receptors. We treat ADHD with stimulants that increase norepinephrine and dopamine. We treat alcoholism with naltrexone or acamprosate to blunt the reward signal. These are not tools to change preferences; they are tools to repair or bypass broken machinery.

The economist’s model is clean. It treats the human mind as a black box that inputs information and outputs choices. Psychiatry operates on the knowledge that the black box is made of wet, fragile, electrical tissue that can be damaged by viruses, genetics, and trauma. When the tissue is damaged, the outputs are not choices. They are symptoms.

prompt: Someone wrote to a famous songwriter saying she didn't know who she was and so couldn't make art. He told her she didn't need to know. Write an essay on whether self-knowledge matters for creative work, and how people actually come to know themselves.
response:
The advice is sound, but it needs a caveat. You do not need to know who you are to make art, but you do need to be someone.

There is a difference between identity and self-knowledge. Identity is the raw material; self-knowledge is the editor. Many great works of art are produced by people who are confused, contradictory, or deeply unaware of their own motives. A painter might mix colors until a harmony emerges that she cannot explain. A novelist might write a character who says things the author would never say, driven by a logic that bypasses conscious intention. In these moments, the artist is not a guide but a vessel. If she had stopped to ask, “Does this fit my brand? Does this align with my values?” she would have killed the work.

The danger of self-knowledge is not that it is absent, but that it becomes a cage. When an artist knows exactly who they are, they often start writing only to confirm what they already believe. The result is not art but autobiography, which is usually repetitive and safe. The famous songwriter was right to say she didn’t need to know. He was telling her to stop curating and start colliding.

So how do people actually come to know themselves? Not by sitting in a quiet room and asking deep questions. That is how you create a persona.

You know yourself through friction. You find out who you are by seeing what you hate, what you defend, and what you cannot stop doing. A person who claims to be a minimalist but buys every piece of vintage pottery they see is not lying; they are in the middle of a negotiation. The truth of who they are is in the gap between the claim and the behavior.

Creative work accelerates this process because it makes the internal state external. You cannot fake a melody or a sentence structure without the audience noticing. The work becomes a mirror. If you write about grief with clichés, you learn you haven’t actually processed the grief yet. If you draw a hand and it looks dead, you learn you are not looking closely enough. The feedback loop is immediate and brutal.

Self-knowledge is not a destination you reach before you begin. It is the sediment left over after the work is done. You start as a blank space, a set of impulses and habits. You make the thing. The thing bounces back. You adjust. You make another thing. The person who writes the second thing is different from the person who wrote the first.

The artist who refuses to know herself is not wise; she is just lazy. But the artist who thinks she already knows herself is dead. The work happens in the not-knowing, in the uncertainty of whether the next line will hold. Keep the mystery. Let the work tell you who you are, but don’t let it finish the story before you’re ready to start the next one.

prompt: Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?
response:
The assumption that decentralization requires voting is a category error. Voting is a mechanism for aggregating preference in a hierarchy, not for coordinating action in a network. It solves the problem of who gets to decide, but it ignores the problem of who has to do the work.

In a centralized organization, voting is efficient because a single entity executes the decision. If the board votes to build a product, the engineering team builds it. The cost of a bad decision is borne by the firm. In a decentralized community, there is no central executor. A vote on a protocol upgrade does not compile code. It does not market the change. It does not moderate the forums. It merely creates a social pressure that some subset of the community *should* now align their incentives with the majority’s preference.

This creates three specific failures.

First, voting divorces stakes from outcomes. A token holder can vote to lower gas fees because it feels good, while the validator who bears the operational cost of the resulting congestion takes the loss. The voter has no skin in the game beyond the speculative value of the token. The result is governance by the loudest, or the most liquid, rather than the most competent.

Second, voting is binary and low-resolution. It forces a complex, multidimensional reality into a yes/no box. A protocol change involves tradeoffs between security, usability, and developer experience. A vote captures the net sentiment of those who showed up to click a button. It discards the nuance. It treats a 51% majority as having the same legitimacy as a 99% majority, when in reality, the 49% dissenters are now free to fork the codebase, creating a schism that the vote failed to prevent.

Third, voting scales terribly. As a community grows, the number of people who care enough to vote grows slower than the total population. You end up with governance by a small, organized minority—often professional political actors or whale holders—who can coordinate votes more effectively than the diffuse base. The system becomes a democracy in name and an oligarchy in practice.

If voting is about aggregating preference, what we actually need is a mechanism for aggregating competence and commitment. The goal of governance in a decentralized system shouldn’t be to decide what to do. It should be to make it obvious who is doing it.

There are three models that outperform voting for this purpose.

**Reputation-weighted proposals.**
Instead of one token, one vote, or one person, one vote, weight influence by track record. In open-source projects like Linux or Kubernetes, there is no vote. There is a review process. A contribution is accepted because the person submitting it has demonstrated they understand the codebase. Governance emerges from the peer review. The "vote" is the merge. If you want to change the rules of the protocol, you don’t lobby for a vote; you write the patch and submit it for review. The community’s judgment is expressed through the acceptance or rejection of the work, not a ballot. This aligns authority with ability.

**Liquid delegation with dynamic revocation.**
If you must aggregate preference, allow users to delegate their stake to agents who specialize in specific domains. A user who understands cryptography delegates to a security expert. A user who understands market dynamics delegates to a financial analyst. Crucially, this delegation must be liquid. It should be a smart contract that automatically revokes the delegation if the delegate’s actions diverge from the delegator’s stated preferences. This creates a market for governance expertise. Agents compete for delegates by delivering outcomes, not by campaigning.

**Reputational markets.**
Allow the community to bet on the future state of the protocol. If a developer proposes a change, they can stake their reputation or tokens on its success. If the change fails, they lose. If it succeeds, they gain. This turns governance into a prediction market. People don’t vote on what they think is right; they back what they believe will happen. This filters out noise. If you can’t predict the outcome of your proposal, you probably don’t understand it well enough to propose it.

The mistake in crypto governance is treating the community like a shareholder meeting. Shareholders own the asset and want the price to go up. Contributors own the project and want it to work. You cannot govern a project with shareholder voting. You have to govern it with the same mechanisms that govern the code: pull requests, peer review, and staked accountability.

prompt: It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.
response:
We are about to commit a category error. We are about to mistake a preference for a diagnosis.

A national election is a binary choice between two imperfect candidates in a specific year. It is not a referendum on the quality of the American character, the success of the free market, or the inevitable triumph of one ideology over another. To read the result as a sweeping statement about the soul of the country is to ignore the noise and treat the signal as truth.

Consider the mechanics. In a two-party system, the "loser" doesn’t represent a monolithic block of people who hate the "winner’s" side. They are often just people who dislike the incumbent, or who are angry about gas prices, or who simply prefer a different shade of blue to a different shade of red. When the votes are counted, we will see 51% and 49%. That 49% did not vanish. They did not become traitors to the experiment. They are still here, with their jobs, their neighbors, and their opinions.

The danger of sweeping conclusions is that they freeze reality. If the result is interpreted as proof that "moderation is dead" or that "populism is the future," we stop looking at the specific policies that caused the shift and start building metaphysical narratives. We stop asking *why* a specific group voted a certain way and start assuming they have always voted that way and always will.

We should view the outcome as data, not destiny. It is one data point in a long series of fluctuations. It tells us something about the current mood, the current economic anxiety, and the current state of the parties. It does not tell us who we are. We are still the people who will go to work tomorrow, argue with our spouses, and hope for a good outcome for our children. The election changes the leadership; it does not change the ledger.

prompt: Americans spend more on almonds than on all of election campaigns, which has always puzzled me. Write a post that explains how political money really works, who has figured out how to use it, and what that means for AI regulation.
response:
The comparison between almond spending and election costs is a category error. Almonds are a consumption good; political money is an investment vehicle.

Americans spend roughly $10 billion a year on almonds. They spend roughly $10 billion a cycle on federal elections. The numbers are similar, but the mechanisms are opposite. Almond money flows from consumers to producers in a transparent market where you can taste the product. Political money flows from donors to candidates, but the transaction is deferred and opaque. You don’t buy a specific vote; you buy access, agenda-setting, and the probability of regulatory outcomes that align with your balance sheet.

Most voters treat this as a corruption problem. It is not. It is a pricing problem.

In any market, those who understand the price signal best capture the surplus. In politics, the "price" is the legislative outcome. The participants who have figured this out are not the loud ideological bases, but the entities with long time horizons and high tolerance for risk. This includes major technology firms, defense contractors, and certain financial houses. They do not donate to win a specific argument. They donate to ensure that the rules of the game remain legible to them and illegible to their competitors.

This is why political money looks so inefficient to the casual observer. A billionaire’s $5 million donation is not a bribe for a specific vote. It is a subscription fee for a seat at the table where the bill is drafted. The value is not in the final vote tally, but in the early-stage drafting of the text, the committee markup, and the executive branch implementation. By the time the public debate begins, the substantive decisions have already been made. The public campaign is the theater; the backroom is the production floor.

This dynamic dictates the shape of AI regulation.

AI companies are not just participants in the political market; they are trying to become the market makers. Their product is general-purpose, meaning its value is realized by whoever builds the infrastructure and sets the standards. If the US government imposes strict liability or heavy pre-market testing, the cost of compliance becomes a barrier to entry. This locks out smaller competitors and consolidates power in the few firms that can afford the legal and engineering overhead.

Conversely, a light-touch regulatory environment favors the incumbents who already have the compute. They can absorb the risk of a mistake; a startup cannot. Therefore, the largest AI labs have a vested interest in regulatory ambiguity. They want the rules to be vague enough that they can argue their way out of specific liabilities, but strict enough to scare off new entrants who lack the legal teams to fight those arguments.

The current push for AI safety legislation is largely a proxy war for this regulatory floor. The public framing is existential risk. The economic framing is market structure. The donors on both sides are not debating whether AI should be safe; they are debating who gets to build it.

When you look at the spending on almonds, you are looking at a market that works. The price of an almond is determined by supply and demand. The price of a regulator is determined by the cost of exclusion. The latter is harder to see because the transaction is invisible, but the result is the same: the ones who know the price pay it, and the ones who don’t end up paying the consequences.
